analysis.one_liner: Funds 1,000 new FBI agents and extra prosecutors to investigate financial-crisis fraud.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced in April 2011, received no committee vote, no floor action, and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have paid for 1,000 new FBI agents, plus forensic experts, additional federal prosecutors, and more Securities and Exchange Commission enforcement staff, all aimed at investigating corporate, securities, and mortgage fraud tied to the 2008 financial crisis. It pointed to the savings-and-loan crisis, where a comparable surge of about 1,000 agents and prosecutors produced more than 1,000 felony convictions of senior insiders, and noted that by the time of the larger 2008 crisis the FBI could field only about 120 agents on mortgage fraud cases. It never moved past its initial referral to two committees.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners and investors who lost money to mortgage and securities fraud, and the broader public, who would gain a real federal effort to identify and criminally prosecute financial-crisis wrongdoing rather than rely on the under-staffed FBI units the bill's findings describe.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Victims of mortgage and securities fraud

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes funding for the FBI to hire 1,000 agents plus forensic experts to investigate corporate, securities, and mortgage fraud tied to U.S. financial markets.
Authorizes additional hires by the Attorney General for prosecutions and by the SEC's Division of Enforcement for related investigations.

The bill's findings argue that the savings-and-loan response, staffed with roughly 1,000 FBI agents and dozens of prosecutors, produced over 1,000 felony convictions of senior insiders, while the FBI had assigned only about 120 agents to mortgage fraud despite calling it an epidemic in 2004.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, through federal appropriations for the new FBI, Justice Department, and SEC positions; the bill leaves the amounts open, authorizing 'such sums as necessary' for fiscal years 2011 through 2014.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes 'such sums as necessary' rather than a dollar cap, leaving the total cost to taxpayers open-ended.

The funding was authorized for fiscal years 2011 through 2014, but the bill was not introduced until April 2011, roughly two and a half years after the crisis peaked, meaning any investigations would start years after the events and could face practical hurdles such as evidence that has gone cold and the passage of time, a mechanism that applies to any late-starting criminal investigation.

Money alone does not guarantee convictions: complex securities cases often fail on proof of intent, so some critics argue a hiring surge would not necessarily replicate the savings-and-loan prosecution record the bill cites as its model.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's approach has a clear precedent: the savings-and-loan surge it cites did produce a large number of insider convictions. The main costs are the open-ended appropriation and the fact that, years after the crisis, cases would be harder to bring than they would have been in 2009. On balance, the potential accountability for wrongdoing that contributed to trillions in losses is large relative to the cost of roughly 1,000 federal positions.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary and Financial Services committees the day it was introduced, neither committee ever took it up, and it expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Marcy Kaptur introduced the bill on April 4, 2011, joined by six original cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the House Financial Services Committee.
The full action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral.
The bill ended the 112th Congress without a vote in either chamber.
It drew 22 cosponsors, 21 Democrats and 1 Republican.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Financial firms and executives who might have faced crisis-era fraud investigations were spared the added 1,000 FBI agents, prosecutors, and SEC enforcement staff the bill would have funded, and no one was held criminally accountable through this route.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Financial firms facing possible fraud cases

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever took place, so no roll-call record exists; support was nearly all Democratic, with 21 of 22 cosponsors Democrats and one Republican.

industries.industry: Large banks, mortgage lenders, and securities firms
industries.note: The bill would fund 1,000 FBI agents, added prosecutors, and more SEC enforcement staff specifically to investigate corporate, securities, and mortgage fraud tied to U.S. financial markets, raising the odds of criminal and enforcement cases against crisis-era insiders. The industry's interest in avoiding those cases runs directly against the public's interest in accountability for losses that helped trigger the crisis.
Federal taxpayers would fund the new hires, with amounts left as 'such sums as necessary' for fiscal years 2011 through 2014 rather than a fixed cap.
